articles.title: Para-cyclist Shaik Arshad fractures leg in fall; medical support missing
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Para-cyclist Shaik Arshad suffered multiple fractures to his previously operated left residual limb after a fall during the men’s time trial at
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Para-cyclist Shaik Arshad suffered multiple fractures to his previously operated left residual limb after a fall during the men’s time trial at the Asian Para Games in Japan on Wednesday, raising questions over the absence of dedicated medical support for the Indian team.Sources told TOI that Arshad, a 2024 Paralympian, crashed in heavy rain at the Izu Velodrome in Shizuoka, sustaining serious injuries to the above-knee amputated limb on which he relies to use his prosthesis. He requires urgent medical attention and surgery, with concerns over the implications for his future mobility.The cycling venue is more than 250 km from Nagoya. Sources said officials had initially asked Arshad and his support staff to travel to Nagoya for hospital admission. Following prolonged discussions, officials agreed to visit the competition venue, where the injured cyclist needed immediate attention.The incident has also raised questions about assurances regarding medical arrangements for the Indian para-cycling contingent. Sources said that at a meeting on Sept 8 at the Sports Authority of India (SAI) office here, involving Arshad’s coach Aditya Verma and SAI officials from the Teams division, with Paralympic Committee of India (PCI) officials participating through phone calls, assurances were apparently given that medical personnel would accompany the team.However, no dedicated medical personnel were available to attend to Arshad at the venue when the accident occurred, sources alleged. Arshad’s coach is now exploring options to travel urgently from Hyderabad to Japan and is arranging a visa to be by the athlete’s side.The injury is particularly serious because it involves Arshad’s residual limb, which is crucial for fitting and using his artificial leg. articles.title: Natalie Nakase Handed $500 Punishment Before Dream Take 2-1 Lead Against the Valkyries in WNBA Finals
articles.summary: The Golden State Valkyries needed answers as the team headed to State Farm Arena to attempt to take the lead in the 2026 WNBA Finals. However, frustration wa...
articles.body:
The Golden State Valkyries needed answers as the team headed to State Farm Arena to attempt to take the lead in the 2026 WNBA Finals. However, frustration was evident in the 97-71 loss to the Atlanta Dream, with one moment involving Valkyries head coach Natalie Nakase standing out, leaving the team with yet another setback during a game the team could not afford to lose.

"Valkyries unwinding a bit here, Natalie Nakase gets called for a tech after the Gabby Williams offensive foul, that latter of which was very unhappy with that call, seemed to signal to the bench to challenge it, which did not happen," Valkyries reporter Kenzo Fukuda noted on X .

The sequence occurred with 48 seconds left in the third quarter. Williams, who was attempting to manufacture anything on offense for a Valkyries team down 68-57, ran into Dream guard Jordin Canada and was called for an offensive foul. She wasn't happy with the call, and neither was Nakase, who was called for a technical foul for arguing with the referees. Unfortunately, the Valkyries did not challenge the call, and Canada converted the technical free throw.

This marks the first technical foul for Nakase this postseason, which means that she will have to pay a $500 fine. The WNBA increased its technical foul penalties this season, and under the new structure, each player and coach is allowed two technical fouls costing $500 each, a third costing $1,000, and the fourth coming with $1,500 in fines and a one-game suspension. Following this, every other technical will result in a one-game suspension.

This came in the middle of the second consecutive loss in the Finals for the Valkyries, who are now down 2-1 in their first Finals appearance against the Dream. Williams was the leading scorer for her team, but struggled to score, logging 15 points on just 5-for-18 from the field and turning the ball over four times.

Angel Reese led the effort for the Dream, who was firing on all cylinders tonight. Reese finished with a 21-point, 12-rebound double-double, with the Dream converting on 49% of their shots, making 10 more than the Valkyries while shooting 12 more free throws than their opponents.

This was the first time the Dream had ever won a Finals game at home, with the team being swept in each of their previous three appearances in 2010, 2011, and 2013

Now, the Valkyries will look to even up the series as they prepare for the fourth game of what has been an electric Finals. Only time will tell which team will take the advantage on October 24.

articles.title: 'Told he was murdered by a fellow athlete': Preeti Pal, India's Asian Para Games medallist, recalls losing training partner earlier this year
articles.summary: India’s Preeti Pal dedicated her second silver medal at the Asian Para Games to her training partner Chirag Tyagi, who was shot dead in May.
articles.body: India’s Preeti Pal dedicated her second silver medal at the Asian Para Games to her training partner Chirag Tyagi, who was shot dead in May. The sprinter remembered Chirag as a younger brother who dreamed of winning medals for India. She believes he would have reached the podium in Nagoya, Japan, had he been alive.Preeti and fellow Indian sprinter Simran Sharma trained with Chirag at Delhi’s Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium under coach Gajendra Singh. His death left both athletes devastated, and memories of him returned as they celebrated their achievements at the Games.“Within a short time, Chirag became our trusted training partner. He was like a younger brother, but he guided us,” Preeti told The Indian Express.She recalled Chirag’s ambition to represent India on the international stage. “I still remember him telling me, ‘Preeti didi, ek din main bhi apki aur Simran didi ki tarah Paralympic aur Asian Games main medal jeetunga aur tirange ko rise hote dekhunga (One day I too will win medals for India in Paralympics and Asian Games and watch the Indian tricolour rise high).’ I dedicate the medals I won to Chirag. He was like a younger brother,” she said.Preeti Pal and Simran shine at the GamesPreeti, who has cerebral palsy, won silver in the women’s 100m T35 final in 13.98 seconds on Wednesday, adding to her silver in the 200m T35 event on Tuesday.Simran, who has impaired vision, won her second gold medal of the Games by claiming the women’s 100m T12 title in an Asian Para Games record time of 12.02 seconds, following her 200m gold.Preeti recalled how she first learned of Chirag’s death while visiting her family in Uttar Pradesh.“Initially, we thought it was an accident. Some hours later, we were told that Chirag was murdered by a fellow athlete. It was a tough phase for us. Chirag stayed in the room opposite us at the stadium. When we are at the stadium, we are reminded of him every day,” she said.Chirag’s family remembers his dreamChirag’s parents, Manoj and Nisha, followed the athletes’ performances from home.His mother said he was inspired by Preeti and Simran and was proud of their achievements. Both athletes, along with their coach, have also stayed in touch with the family and provided financial support.Chirag had qualified for the Para Asian Games in the men’s 400m and 1500m T12 events after winning gold at the Indian Open Para Athletics International Championship in Bengaluru in May.Preeti remembered how Chirag had cheered her on when she won the 100m T35 title at the World Para Athletics Championships in New Delhi last year.“We had a deep bond,” she said, adding that she regretted never tying a rakhi on his wrist. “Winning medals gives me joy. I wish Chirag were with us to share the joy.”Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: China edge USA to women’s team gold at Gymnastics World Championships
articles.summary: China finished 0.233 points ahead of the Americans, denying them a chance to win an eighth consecutive team gold.
articles.body:
China have denied the United States an eighth consecutive women’s team title at the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships as Qiu Qiyuan sealed a dramatic victory with the final routine.

Qiu needed to score more than 12.600 points in the closing floor routine to give her country gold and did just enough with 12.833 on Wednesday.

The USA last failed to win gold when they were beaten by Russia at the 2010 championships, but were left to count the cost of several errors on the balance beam in Rotterdam.

China, who also led the way in qualifying, finished with 165.764 points, edging out the Americans by 0.233 overall.

Japan were a further 1.468 points behind as they completed the podium ahead of fourth-placed France.

USA superstar Simone Biles, a 23-time world champion including five times in the team competition, is taking a break from the sport and has not competed since the 2024 Paris Olympics, where she won three gold medals.

The reigning champions took a healthy lead at the halfway stage, helped by strong vault and uneven bars routines by Skye Blakely, the only gymnast on the team who was part of the quintet that won their seventh consecutive title in 2023.

But 18-year-old Caylor Dulcy stumbled on the beam, scoring just 12.333, as the Americans were outscored by more than four points on the apparatus by their rivals.

Zhang Qingying, who topped beam qualifying, in particular made them pay with a sparkling performance that earned her 15.066 points.

The Chinese were put under pressure on the floor, but Qiu held her nerve to secure their first women’s team world crown since 2006.

The championships continue in the Netherlands on Thursday as Japan’s Daiki Hashimoto defends his men’s all-around title, with a big challenge expected from his compatriot and Olympic champion Shinnosuke Oka.

Japan took the men’s team title on Tuesday, pipping Russia and China.

articles.title: Hip injury, viral fever, vomiting: How Paralympic champion Praveen Kumar fought back to win Asian Para Games gold
articles.summary: Praveen Kumar had to fight more than his rivals to win gold at the Asian Para Games.
articles.body: Praveen Kumar had to fight more than his rivals to win gold at the Asian Para Games. The reigning Paralympic champion was dealing with a hip injury that had affected his jumping form for months. He was also battling fever, cold and cough during the competition in Japan.Despite these challenges, Praveen cleared 2.05m to win the men’s high jump T44/64 gold medal with a Games record on Wednesday. His jump also bettered the previous Asian Para Games record of 1.95m in the T44 category. Banti won silver with a personal best of 1.92m, while Uzbekistan’s Temurbek Giyazov took bronze with 1.86m.Praveen fights illness to win goldPraveen was not at his best physically when he competed at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletics Stadium. He had contracted a viral fever a few days after arriving in Japan and had been struggling with fever and a cough for most of the week.He even vomited and suffered coughing spells between attempts. However, he continued competing and secured his second successive Asian Para Games title.“With the fever, cold and cough, training here became a difficult task, but I continued with short breaks. While my body felt fine during the final, my first jump gave me a severe headache. The mucus from my blocked nose and throat was also troubling me. I wanted to better my Asian Para Games record, and to achieve that in such a condition is a special feeling for me,” Kumar tells The Indian Express.How a hip injury affected his jumpingPraveen had already proved himself on the biggest stage. At the Paris Paralympics, he won gold with a career-best jump of 2.08m, improving on the silver medal he won at the Tokyo Paralympics. His 2.08m jump remains the Asian record.However, a hip injury slowed his progress after that success. He won bronze at the World Para Athletics Championships in New Delhi last September, clearing 2.00m despite the injury.The problem continued to affect his performances, and he could not cross the 2.05m mark in the months that followed. A jump of 2.03m on the national circuit two months ago gave him hope that he was getting back to his best.Praveen was born with a deformity in his left leg. The hip injury made it harder for him to generate the power needed to take off during a jump.“I suffered a ligament tear in my hip last year, which meant I could not generate enough power from the hip during take-off. When I planted my right knee to jump, my hip would hurt a lot and I could not generate the lift. The first focus was to recover, followed by jumping exercises to strengthen the hip muscles and short sprints to build strength in my left leg. Not having a jump close to 2.05m was a bit demotivating, but I knew I had to recover and train fully to regain my old form,” Kumar says.The learningPraveen first learnt about high jump by watching videos online. He has been training under coach Satyapal Singh since 2018. When the injury disrupted his progress, the coach focused on helping him stay positive while rebuilding strength in his hip.“Praveen’s strength has always been his smooth take-off and clearance in the Fosbury Flop technique. While able-bodied high jumpers have to bend the non-leading knee during take-off, his deformity in the left leg means he does not have to worry about that aspect. He had good speed on the runway even at a young age and was also good at running the curve. His back-leaning position and flexibility during clearance were always good, and we only had to improve them with time," Singh said."He is a short high jumper, but he compensates for that disadvantage with almost perfect technique. After the injury, I knew rebuilding strength in his hip would take time, but I kept reminding him of his best jumps. I did not want him to think negatively,” he said.Who is Praveen Kumar's inspiration?With another Asian Para Games gold medal secured, Praveen has already started thinking about the next big challenge: defending his Paralympic title at the Los Angeles Games.One athlete he continues to learn from is Canadian high jumper Derek Drouin, who won gold at the 2016 Rio Olympics with a jump of 2.38m.Praveen studies Drouin’s technique, particularly how he builds speed during his run-up and converts it into upward lift at take-off. He is also working to strengthen his left leg and make changes to his approach.“For the last seven to eight years, I have watched videos of Derek Drouin competing at the Rio Olympics almost daily. I closely observe how he generates explosiveness from his run-up and then almost stops at take-off to create vertical lift. Even though my left leg is not as strong as my right, I have been working on building its strength. I am also aiming to increase my run-up by one or two steps. It will take time to adjust, but I am confident I can surpass my personal best next season and work towards defending my title at the LA Paralympics,” Kumar says.What are the T44 and T64 categories?The T44 and T64 categories are often combined in para athletics events to ensure enough athletes can compete.T64 is for athletes who run using a prosthetic lower limb. articles.title: Wrong national anthems played three times at Asian Para Games in Japan
articles.summary: The Iranian national anthem was played for athletes from Taiwan and Mongolia, prompting Nagoya’s mayor to apologise.
articles.body:
Wrong national anthems were played three times at the Asian Para Games in Japan’s Nagoya this week, prompting the mayor to apologise weeks after the city hosted the mishap-plagued Asian Games .

Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa apologised on Wednesday for the latest error, which occurred despite officials’ pledges to implement steps to prevent mistakes, including playing the correct national anthems.

“These things happened during the Asian Games, so, of course, the operations were reviewed and examined based on the lessons learned. The fact that it happened again is really just unacceptable,” the mayor said at a news conference.

The Asian Para Games is taking place in the central Japanese hub city through Saturday, featuring about 4,000 athletes and officials in 18 sports.

On Monday, a Taiwanese athlete won a men’s para taekwondo competition, but the Iranian anthem was played in its entirety, according to Nagoya officials at the mayor’s news conference.

Officials realised their mistake after the ceremony, they said.

The Iranian anthem was played again that day during a women’s para taekwondo ceremony as a Mongolian competitor was receiving the gold medal, according to the city.

The incorrect music was stopped after the Mongolian delegation pointed out the error.

Organisers then played the Mongolian anthem after the music was provided by the delegation, Nagoya officials said.

Separately on Monday, officials broadcast the South Korean anthem for about five seconds instead of the Chinese one before a sitting volleyball match between China and Iran.

“It is unacceptable, or rather, it’s painful. I am very sorry about it,” the mayor said, adding that he felt the tournament was otherwise progressing smoothly.

The Asian Games, which concluded in early October, faced heavy criticism for shortcomings ranging from inadequate accommodations for athletes to the playing of wrong national anthems.

On September 18, organisers played North Korea’s national anthem for the South Korean hockey team.

articles.title: Sheetal Devi strikes double gold again! Indian archer repeats 2023 Asian Para Games medal feat in 2026
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Indian para-archer Sheetal Devi once again proved her mettle on the biggest continental stage, winning two gold medals at the Asian Para Games
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Indian para-archer Sheetal Devi once again proved her mettle on the biggest continental stage, winning two gold medals at the Asian Para Games for the second consecutive edition after clinching the women's individual compound title on Thursday.The 19-year-old armless archer from Jammu and Kashmir produced a stunning comeback to defeat Singapore's Alim Nur Syahidah 142-139 in the final at Okazaki Chuo Sogo Park Multipurpose Square, successfully defending the individual title she won in Hangzhou in 2023.The victory completed a memorable double-gold day for Sheetal, who had teamed up with Toman Kumar to win the compound mixed team gold earlier in the day. She also secured a silver medal in the women's compound doubles event alongside Odisha's quadruple amputee archer Payal Nag.With three medals — two golds and a silver — Sheetal has replicated her medal tally from the 2023 Asian Para Games, where she also won two gold medals and a silver to announce herself as one of India's brightest para-sporting talents.Sheetal turns the tide to defend individual crownSheetal had to dig deep to retain her individual crown, with Alim initially putting the Indian under pressure in their gold medal clash.The Singaporean archer established a four-point advantage after the opening two ends, leaving Sheetal with plenty of work to do. However, the Indian mounted an extraordinary recovery, firing six 10s, including three Xs — arrows landing closest to the centre of the target — across the next two ends.The remarkable sequence helped Sheetal overturn the deficit and take a two-point lead into the final end, setting up a tense finish.With the gold medal on the line, Sheetal maintained her composure, scoring three 9s for 27 points in the final end. Alim, meanwhile, managed scores of 9, 8 and 9 for 26 points, allowing the Indian to seal a 142-139 victory.The triumph was particularly significant as it came less than a couple of hours after Sheetal had won the mixed team gold with Toman, underlining her ability to deliver under pressure across multiple events.Three medals again, just like HangzhouSheetal's campaign in 2026 has followed a familiar pattern from her breakthrough performance at the 2023 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, China.At the previous edition, she won gold in the women's individual compound event and the compound mixed team competition alongside Rakesh Kumar. She also claimed silver in the women's team event with Sarita.Three years later, Sheetal repeated that medal-winning feat, this time collecting individual and mixed team gold medals alongside a silver with Payal Nag in the women's compound doubles.The Indian duo had topped the ranking round in the doubles event but lost 141-150 to China's Xueqing Xu and Jing Zhao in the final on Wednesday.Sheetal's latest triumph further strengthens her reputation as a leading figure in Indian para-archery. Having already made history in Hangzhou by becoming the first Indian woman to win two gold medals in a single edition of the Asian Para Games, she has now successfully repeated the feat in 2026.At just 19, Sheetal continues to turn extraordinary personal determination into landmark sporting achievements, delivering another golden chapter for India on the para-sporting stage.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Angel Reese shines again as Dream down Valkyries to lead WNBA Finals
articles.summary: Atlanta’s Reese has become the only woman in history to record consecutive double-doubles in three WNBA Finals games.
articles.body:
Angel Reese produced another dominant all-round display as the Atlanta Dream routed the Golden State Valkyries 97-71 to take a 2-1 lead in the best-of-seven WNBA Finals.

Three-time WNBA All-Star and reigning defensive player of the year Reese followed up her 30-point display in game two on Monday to once again lead the Atlanta scoring with 21 points.

The 24-year-old also reigned on the defensive end, finishing with 12 rebounds and three steals to neutralise Golden State’s offence.

Additionally, Reese also became the youngest player in WNBA Finals to record more than 20 points and 10 rebounds in consecutive games.

Reese was one of five Dream players to finish in double-figures, with Rhyne Howard adding 16 points and Naz Hillmon 15 points.

Gabby Williams led Golden State’s scoring with 15 points.

“We feel good – we’re still pissed that we lost the first game,” Reese said afterwards. “We know how good we are; we know our identity.

“We’re all happy for sure, but it’s going to take more. The job is not finished so we’re going to keep going,” added Reese, who is the only woman in history to record consecutive double-doubles in her first three WNBA Finals games.

“It feels good when you’re in the finals – when you can do it at the highest level; this is what I live for,” Reese said.

Earlier, Reese picked up where she left off in game two, draining a three-pointer to help Atlanta take a 22-12 lead as the first quarter drew to a close.

Golden State narrowed the deficit to six points at half-time and drew level at 48-48 early in the third quarter.

But Atlanta responded with an 8-0 run to pull clear again, and took a stranglehold on the contest after outscoring Golden State 25-17 in the third to lead by 14 points heading into the final period.

Atlanta stretched the lead to 21 points late in the fourth quarter to all but ice the contest, and the points kept flowing as the Dream delivered a statement victory.

Game four takes place in Atlanta on Saturday.

Both teams are chasing a first WNBA title. The Dream have come up empty in three prior trips to the Finals, most recently in 2013.

The Valkyries, who last year became the first WNBA expansion franchise to reach the playoffs in their inaugural season, are now contending for the title in their second.

articles.summary: India enjoyed a successful day at the Asian Para Games on Thursday, with Anjanaben Bumbadiya winning gold and Jayanti Behera taking silver in the women’s
articles.body: India enjoyed a successful day at the Asian Para Games on Thursday, with Anjanaben Bumbadiya winning gold and Jayanti Behera taking silver in the women’s 400m T47 event.Anjanaben clocked 59.97 seconds to finish first, becoming the only athlete in the four-runner race to break the one-minute mark.Jayanti finished second in 1:00.65, while Thailand’s Sasirawan Inthachot claimed bronze in 1:02.58.Tejalben Damor also added to India’s medal tally, winning silver in the women’s 400m T12 event with a time of 57.60 seconds.It was her second medal of the Games after taking bronze in the 200m T12 race.Sheetal Devi wins two gold medalsArmless archer Sheetal Devi enjoyed another memorable outing, winning gold in both the women’s individual compound and mixed team events. She teamed up with Toman Kumar to beat Indonesia 151-148 in the mixed team final, giving India its first archery gold medal at the Games.Later, Sheetal returned to the range for the individual final against Singapore’s Alim Nur Syahidah. Despite trailing by four points early on, the reigning world champion fought back with accurate shots to win 142-139. The victory marked her second consecutive individual gold at the Asian Para Games.Sheetal, who uses her feet and legs to position the bow and her shoulder and jaw to draw and release the string, finished the day with three medals, including a silver in the women’s compound team event won on Wednesday.However, Toman missed out on an individual medal after losing the men’s bronze playoff to China’s Zhang Yicheng 139-148.Swati Chaudhary creates history with silverSwati Chaudhary became India’s first-ever medallist in the W1 archery category after winning silver in the women’s individual event. articles.summary: India swept all three medals in the men's high jump T63 final at the Asian Para Games 2026 on Thursday, with Shailesh Kumar winning gold ahead of Varun
articles.body: India swept all three medals in the men's high jump T63 final at the Asian Para Games 2026 on Thursday, with Shailesh Kumar winning gold ahead of Varun Bhati and Rahul Saroha at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium in Japan.Shailesh cleared 1.89m to set a new Asian Para Games record, breaking the previous mark of 1.80m set by India's Sharad Kumar at the 2014 edition in Incheon, South Korea.Shailesh was in close competition with Varun until the bar was raised to 1.84m. He then cleared 1.87m and 1.89m to move ahead and secure the gold medal with a new Games record.Former Paralympic bronze medallist Varun took silver with a season's best jump of 1.84m, while Rahul won bronze after clearing 1.81m.With this result, India repeated its podium sweep from the 2022 edition in the men's high jump T42/T63 event, once again claiming all three medals.The T63 classification is for athletes with an above-knee amputation or limb deficiency, who compete using a lower-limb prosthesis with a knee joint for running and jumping. The Indian high jump trio usually competes in the T42 category, which covers lower-limb deficiency, leg-length difference, impaired muscle power or limited passive movement affecting hip and knee function.The Philippines' Edwin Enguito, Myanmar's Zaw Min Tun and Pakistan's Muhammad Nadeem finished fourth, fifth and sixth respectively.This was India's third clean sweep at the Games. articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: England head coach Brian McDermot blasts 'harsh' format and explains Mikey Lewis absence
articles.summary: England take on France in Perth on Saturday (7.35am) in their second Rugby League World Cup fixture, having been thrashed by Tonga in opener; Coach Brian McDermott discussed World Cup format and Mikey Lewis' continued absence ahead of weekend clash
articles.body:
Last Saturday's loss to Tonga means England must hope Tonga beat Samoa in their final group game next week in order to stand any realistic chance of reaching the semi-finals.

That scenario would leave England and Samoa to be separated by points difference - a particularly tough ask for McDermott's men given the Samoans started their campaign with a crushing 78-4 win over France.

"The jeopardy is losing one game is so harsh, it's almost like we don't get another chance to straighten things out," said McDermott, whose side face the French in their second group game in Perth on Saturday.

"There's still a slim chance that we get through, and that's something we're focusing on, and we're really determined. It's just harsh that we have to take a standing eight count in the first round."

This year's World Cup was reduced to 10 men's teams after France pulled out of hosting the event in 2023, resulting in a complicated, partial cross-group format which means one of the top five nations will be eliminated at the first stage.

In contrast, favourites Australia and New Zealand are effectively guaranteed to reach the last four after being placed in a conventional, four-team Group A alongside Fiji and the Cook Islands.

McDermott added: "New Zealand have lost their first game as well, but they're going to get another go at it and the likelihood is they'll qualify, so their destiny is not lying in other people's hands.

"That's not the position we find ourselves in. There's no frustration, all I'm recognising in that the jeopardy is really harsh. We knew that for us to go through, we had to go and beat Tonga."

'Lewis has shown humility in camp - we have considered changes'

In his squad to face France on Saturday, McDermott has stuck with the same 19-man group that were thrashed 30-12 by Tonga, with a late alteration seeing Matty Ashton start in place of Zach Eckersley on the wing.

There remains no place for Hull KR star Lewis, who is named a reserve and not in the starting team nor on the bench.

The 25-year-old, who won 2024's Man of Steel, has picked up eight caps so far in his career, but only started three of them.

"He [Lewis] is good, it was a frustrating end to the season for him, but he won a World Club Challenge at the start of the year," McDermott said.

"He's been great round the camp, he knows his role. He's shown a lot of humility in the camp, as have a few other players.

"Mikey Lewis is a tremendous player and you've got to wonder whether he'd give us something that we haven't got.

"For sure, it has been considered [change at half-back], but I thought George (Williams) was good against Tonga.

"I think George has been unfairly assessed and I thought Harry Smith was really good. We were co-ordinated both in yardage attack and good ball attack.

"We got held up over the line four times in the game and there was a try-saver from Tonga holding up Herbie Farnworth."

England: AJ Brimson, Dom Young, Hugo Savala, Herbie Farnworth, Matty Ashton, George Williams, Harry Smith, Max King, Brad O'Neill, Luke Thompson, Junior Nsemba, Kai Pearce-Paul, Victor Radley.

Interchange: Jez Litten, Ben Currie, Ethan Havard, Sam Walters, Jack Welsby, Zach Eckersley.

France: Arthur Mourgue, Guillermo Aispuro-Bichet, Latrell Siegwalt, Roméo Tropis, Benjamin Laguerre, Thomas Lacans, Théo Fages, Romain Navarrete, Amir Bourouh, Julian Bousquet, Arthur Romano, Mathieu Jussaume, Benjamin Garcia (c).

Interchange: César Rougé, Lambert Belmas, Mathieu Cozza, Louis Grossemy.

articles.title: Changes Triple H Must Make to Excite Fans for WWE WrestleMania 43
articles.summary: WrestleMania is supposed to be the biggest event on the calendar, delivering unforgettable matches, career-defining moments and surprises that keep the WWE Universe talking long after the two-day event ends.
articles.body:
WrestleMania is supposed to be the biggest event on the calendar, delivering unforgettable matches, career-defining moments and surprises that keep the WWE Universe talking long after the two-day event ends.

With the Road to WrestleMania on the horizon, WWE chief content officer Triple H and his creative team have a chance to make the marquee show feel special with a few key storytelling and character-development changes.

From elevating new stars to making every championship match count, here are changes that could help make WrestleMania 43 an event fans won't want to miss.

Debating Triple H's Obsession With WarGames Match 👨‍⚖️

WrestleMania needs fresh faces in its biggest matches, and Triple H should use the months leading up to the event to establish new main-event contenders.

While established stars will always have a place on the card, relying on the same handful of names year after year risks making the biggest matches feel predictable.

WWE should give rising talent meaningful rivalries, memorable victories and enough television time to convince fans they belong alongside the company's biggest attractions.

The road to WrestleMania is the perfect opportunity to change the roster's hierarchy and introduce potential headliners to a broader audience.

Instead of waiting until the final weeks to push someone into a major match, WWE should build momentum through consistent storytelling and performances that make fans invest in their success.

WrestleMania 43 should feature stars who are ready to take the next step, giving audiences a reason to be excited about the company's future as well as its present.

Let Established Stars Put Over the Next Generation

Creating new main eventers means little if WWE refuses to let them win the matches that matter most.

Triple H needs to be willing to book rising stars to defeat established names cleanly on the WrestleMania stage, giving them a career-defining moment that can change their standing overnight.

Protecting every veteran through interference, controversial finishes or immediate rematches can undermine the very talent WWE is trying to elevate.

Established Superstars can still play important roles without winning every major match, and passing the torch can benefit everyone involved. An emerging wrestler defeating a respected veteran at WrestleMania gives fans a memorable moment while creating new possibilities for the months ahead.

WWE should use WrestleMania 43 to establish who belongs at the top of the card, rather than simply reinforcing the existing pecking order.

WrestleMania has grown into a massive two-night spectacle, but adding more matches does not automatically make the event better.

An overloaded card can leave fans exhausted, shorten matches that deserve more time and reduce the impact of important moments. Triple H should prioritize quality over quantity, ensuring every contest has a clear purpose and enough time to deliver.

Both nights should have a distinct identity, with a carefully paced lineup that builds toward the biggest matches and strongest moments. WWE doesn't need to squeeze every available Superstar onto the card if it comes at the expense of meaningful storytelling or match quality.

A more focused WrestleMania season could leave fans remembering the best performances and surprises instead of wondering when the show would finally end.

Give Midcard Championships Meaningful Stories

The men's and women's intercontinental, United States and tag team titles should feel like important prizes at WrestleMania, not obligatory additions to the card.

Triple H should invest in compelling rivalries for these championships, give challengers clear motivations and let conflicts develop over several weeks. Fans are more likely to care about a title match when the wrestlers have a personal history and something meaningful to prove.

WWE also has an opportunity to use these matches to showcase performers who might not be involved in the world-title picture but can still deliver some of the night's best action. Instead of relying on multi-person matches with limited buildup, the company should give its secondary championships distinct stories and meaningful stakes.

When WrestleMania arrives, every championship match should feel like a major opportunity, not a brief detour between the main events.

articles.title: Henri Schoeman says viral 2016 win over Brownlees led to decade of abuse
articles.summary: Henri Schoeman, who took a viral 2016 Triathlon World Series Grand Final over Jonny Brownlee, reveals the decade of abuse in the race's aftermath.
articles.body:
Henri Schoeman, who won a viral 2016 Triathlon World Series Grand Final in which Jonny Brownlee was helped over the line by his brother Alistair, says he has received a decade of abuse since the race.

South African Schoeman, then 25, was vying for the lead with Jonny Brownlee on the final run leg and overtook the dehydrated and exhausted Briton with 700m to go in Cozumel, Mexico.

With the help of third-placed Alistair, Brownlee finished second, short of the victory which would have secured him the world title in the overall standings.

"It was one of the biggest wins in my career, but for the last 10 years it has been overshadowed by something I have never publicly spoken about," Schoeman wrote on Instagram. , external

"Every time this video goes viral I receive messages and comments blaming me for what happened, attacking me and sometimes even attacking my family."

Schoeman said he came into the race determined to prove a point after some had questioned whether his Olympic bronze in 2016 - behind the Brownlees - was a one-off.

He said long-distance racing has featured many examples of athletes misjudging their pace or fuelling strategy and 'hitting the wall' close to the finish line.

He cited Norwegian Solveig Lovseth, whose Ironman world title defence this month ended when she collapsed in the final mile , external when leading the race.

"Athletes lead for hours only to collapse in the final stages," Schoeman said. "That is the brutal reality of endurance sport.

"The finish line is where winners are made and in Cozumel I crossed that finish line first.

"What people don't see is the impact of the last 10 years of hate and abuse have had on me and my family.

"I know what happened that day and what it took to win and I have absolutely no regrets on how I raced.

"It was one of my biggest victories and, after 10 years, I am finally ready to be proud of it again."

Schoeman, who won Commonwealth Games gold in 2018, finished 20th at the 2024 Olympics and second in the African Championships this month.

articles.title: “We can close F2 down”: Ralf Schumacher warns veterans Fernando Alonso and Lewis Hamilton are blocking F1 opportunities for young drivers
articles.summary: Ralf Schumacher has raised concerns about the growing lack of opportunities for young drivers in Formula 1.
articles.body: Ralf Schumacher has raised concerns about the growing lack of opportunities for young drivers in Formula 1. The former F1 driver believes veterans such as Fernando Alonso and Lewis Hamilton continuing to race into their 40s could make it harder for rising stars to reach the top level.Schumacher has questioned the future of Formula 2 if established drivers continue competing for so long. He believes the sport must consider how its current stars’ longevity affects junior champions waiting for their chance.Ralf Schumacher says F1 should shut down F2 if veterans race until 45Ralf Schumacher believes Formula 1’s growing number of experienced drivers is creating a bottleneck for young talent. He made his position clear while discussing the careers of Alonso, Hamilton and other veterans.“If everyone races until they are 45, we can actually close F2 down. At some point, there is simply no room left for the young drivers”, he said.The German acknowledged that seeing older drivers remain competitive is impressive. However, he believes their extended careers can also create an unfair situation for younger racers hoping to secure an F1 seat.Schumacher pointed to the careers of Kimi Antonelli and Max Verstappen while explaining his concerns. Both drivers entered Formula 1 at a young age. He questioned what would happen if the current generation followed Alonso and Hamilton by continuing to race well into their 40s.He added, “It was like that a very, very long time ago, until Michael effectively entered Formula 1 and proved what fitness and youth can achieve in combination. Training was redefined back then – and, to be fair, it was down to him. Then that trend carried on, and Michael [Schumacher] was the exception in that he actually made a comeback. Today, Nico Hulkenberg is approaching 40, Lewis Hamilton is over 40, Alonso too. It’s all great; I think it’s lovely that the drivers are staying in Formula 1 for so long.”Despite appreciating their longevity, Schumacher believes the sport must also consider the drivers waiting in the junior categories.“I’d say I still find it a bit unfair, also towards the next generation. I mean, look at the drivers - when did Kimi Antonelli start, or Max Verstappen - when did he start? If you really think it through, if they were to carry on racing until they’re 45, then you might as well shut down Formula 2 straight away”, he continued.Formula 2 is designed to prepare young drivers for Formula 1. However, winning the championship does not guarantee an immediate promotion.Gabriel Bortoleto secured an F1 seat after winning the 2024 F2 championship. Several other champions have had to wait longer for their opportunities.Schumacher has also questioned whether modern F1 cars make it easier for older drivers to remain competitive. articles.title: El Team Dalma de Abu Dhabi ficha a Arturo Coello y Agustín Tapia para las Hexagon World Series
articles.standfirst: Golpe en la mesa del nuevo equipo de Emiratos Árabes Unidos reuniendo a los dos números 1
articles.summary: Golpe en la mesa del nuevo equipo de Emiratos Árabes Unidos reuniendo a los dos números 1
articles.body: La Hexagon World Series 2027 comienza una nueva era con la incorporación de un nuevo equipo a la competición: Team Dalma, una formación con sede en Abu Dhabi, Emiratos Árabes Unidos, que aterriza en el circuito con una declaración de intenciones de primer nivel. Sus dos primeros fichajes son nada menos que Arturo Coello y Agustín Tapia, actuales números uno del mundo de Premier Padel. La llegada de ambos jugadores convierte al Team Dalma en uno de los grandes protagonistas del nuevo proyecto de la competición por equipos que arranca en 2027 con cuatro pruebas (Madrid, Norte América, Escandinavia y Abu Dhabi). El fichaje de los 'Golden Boys' supone un golpe sobre la mesa del nuevo equipo que entra entre los 8 en sustitución del RL9 Team. Para Agustín Tapia, el cambio, por tanto supone además abandonar las filas del que fuera equipo de Robert Lewandowski. Al no continuar en la próxima edición, el jugador argentino de Catamarca emprende una nueva etapa en el proyecto de Abu Dhabi, donde se convierte en una de las grandes piezas de una formación en la que tendrá al lado a su compañero habitual durante el año. Coello, por tanto, también cambia de aires para unirse a Dalma. El jugador español ha sido una de las grandes estrellas de Team Bella Puerto Rico desde su estreno en Hexagon en 2024, pero ahora cambiará de aires para formar, sin dudas, la pareja más temible del nuevo circuito. Para la categoría femenina, Giulia Dal Pozzo, italiana de 21 años que sigue creciendo y Premier Padel, estará junto a la portuguesa Sofía Araujo representando al equipo emiratí. La apuesta del Dalma Team por reunir a los dos números uno del mundo refleja desde el primer momento la ambición del nuevo equipo. Abu Dhabi se incorpora a la Hexagon World Series con un proyecto capaz de atraer a las principales figuras del pádel y con dos nombres que garantizan protagonismo tanto dentro de la pista como en el crecimiento internacional de la competición.

articles.title: Washington high school girl walks off starting line alone in protest of trans runner, ending her season
articles.summary: Elise Bierer walked off the start line alone at the district meet, sacrificing her shot at regionals to protest a transgender athlete in girls sports.
articles.body: There was no group to stand with her in solidarity. No teammate to lean on. We've seen other girls cross country runners in Washington state walk off the start line in protest of having to compete against a boy, but Elise Bierer was the first to do it all by herself. It happened Wednesday during the Greater St. Helens League District Meet, where a runner for Camas High was competing as a girl after starting the year racing against the boys. And when the gun went off for the women's varsity race, Bierer walked off the line toward her mother, Sheona, who embraced her tearful daughter. DAD BANNED FROM SCHOOL GROUNDS AFTER PROTESTING TRANS RUNNER COMPETING AGAINST HIS DAUGHTER This was certainly not how Elise, a sophomore at Battle Ground High, pictured her season ending when the school year began. She was the second-fastest female cross country runner on her team, and almost certainly would have advanced to regionals had she participated Wednesday. But as her mom explained, Bierer had been anticipating a moment like this for a couple of years, and was prepared to stand â or more precisely, walk â on principle. "Before she entered high school â she's a sophomore â I told her that it's a real possibility that this could come into play, that she might be forced to race against a male. When we talked about that, she said if that were to happen, she would stand up for what was right and just not compete," said Sheona Bierer, speaking for a daughter who didn't feel comfortable being interviewed. So two Tuesdays ago, when Battle Ground met Camas in a dual meet, Bierer and other teammates decided that they were simply not going to compete. But there really wasn't a whole lot on the line in that race. This time, though, it was districts. This time, a protest meant saying sayonara to her season. A CROSS COUNTRY RUNNER SWITCHED TO THE GIRLS TEAM MIDSEASON, PARENTS VOICE THEIR DISAPPROVAL AT MEET Sheona said Elise and other Battle Ground girls who didn't want to compete against the biological boy were pressured into running in the JV race Wednesday. This would maximize Battle Ground's chances of finishing in the top three of four teams to advance to regionals. Two things, though. 1) Because of all this controversy, only five Battle Ground racers even showed up for Wednesday's women's varsity race (the other three teams had seven apiece). And 2) Elise felt it was her rightful place to line up with the varsity. She'd earned that position. Sheona said that the initial plan was for other Battle Ground girls to walk off the start line with Elise. But those plans changed before the race, leaving Elise to make a statement all by herself. What was that like to watch as a mom? I asked. "I'm super proud. I'm still overwhelmed," said Sheona, adding that Elise has been running since sixth grade but would not return to the team next year if she had to run against the Camas boy. "I know this is really hard, but I love her, and I'm so glad that she's going to stand up for what's right, even when everybody else is walking away from what's right and chose to buckle under pressure." Sheona said Elise didn't inform Battle Ground coach Patricia Tester of her plan for fear of being relegated to JV. I attempted to ask Tester about Bierer after the race â and about the exodus of female runners from her team â but she wouldn't even offer a no comment. Then, another Battle Ground coach stepped in. "Go away, please. That's my comment," he said. I told him I was just trying to get answers about an athlete who protested. "Leave the kids alone," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE I can't speak for other writers â and there were quite a few of them out there Wednesday â but I'd love to leave the kids alone. Unfortunately, Washington state law allows high school males to compete against high school females if they identify as the latter â leaving myriad girls distressed. The Camas boy finished second out of 26 runners Wednesday, officially displacing a biological girl from competing in regionals â as only 21 can advance. He also helped lead his Papermakers to first place in the women's varsity team results. Earlier this season, he finished first in a varsity dual meet despite placing 76th among boys a couple weeks prior. People are tired of this â and not just those on opposing teams. Eight days ago, about a dozen of the runner's own female teammates walked off the starting line for Camas. One of them was Holly Burns, who spoke at a pre-meet rally attended by scores of supporters of Initiative 638, a Nov. 3 ballot measure in Washington state that would require K-12 athletes to compete according to their sex at birth. She had no idea her walking off the start line would spark the reaction it has â but it helped turn Wednesday's meet into the kind of media spectacle rarely seen in high school cross country. "When I was talking about it with the girls, we were kind of like 'what's the point of even doing this?' It's not like it was going to change anything," said Burns, who, according to one parent, is one of 18 girls from Camas to have quit the team entirely. "But it seems like it definitely made a wave." This won't be the only OutKick column from Wednesday's meet. There is much more to be written about the adults who are finally showing the courage that's been almost exclusive to the high schoolers so far. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But this one is dedicated to Elise Bierer, who showed what real integrity looks like. Her coach wants us to leave her alone. No. Not when she had the guts to stand alone.

articles.title: Strength in Variety: How Mizzou’s frontcourt protects the paint by committee
articles.summary: With its point-of-attack personnel upgraded, Bryson Tiller, Jaylen Carey, and Trent Burns provide Dennis Gates three distinct interior toolsets to complete t...
articles.body:
Under coach Dennis Gates, patience defined Missouri's search for a center.

When the transfer portal opened, the Tigers' staff devoted early resources elsewhere to shore up or reboot their roster. Then, usually in late April or May, the program would rummage around for an affordable veteran, a process that turned up the likes of Connor Vanover, Josh Gray or Shawn Phillips Jr. At the same time, MU might take a swing on a project like Jordan Butler, Peyton Marshall or Trent Burns.

Four years in, neither approach has cultivated much continuity.

So, Gates changed tack this spring. He moved swiftly to secure Jaylen Carey as a rugged depth piece and committed real resources to mining Bryson Tiller's upside. Meanwhile, MU kept Burns in the fold rather than abandoning the developmental route.

Ideally, Tiller makes the pecking order easy by claiming the bulk of the minutes. But with Carey and Burns on hand, Gates has some latitude to tailor the job rather than ask one player to handle everything. And that's useful because operating at center involves more than occupying the lane and waiting to contest a shot. Often, the job starts when something goes wrong farther from the basket.

As we've noted before , tMU's late-season slide wasn't tied to a lack of size. The trouble started on the ball. The Tigers couldn't consistently prevent guards and wings from turning the corner, forcing the back line to absorb one breakdown after another. Eventually, it couldn't plug every leak. Starting in late January, the results around the rim made that clear.

At least Gates has more ways to handle that pressure. Bryson Tiller, Jaylen Carey and Trent Burns bring different tools to the job, giving MU some flexibility in how it protects the paint.

There's a catch, though. None carried a starter's workload at center last season. As a group, they averaged slightly more than 16 minutes per game, operating as clear backups or deep-bench options. Their court time was relatively consistent, but hardly extensive.

Does that mean a larger burden is beyond them? Not necessarily. But we're dealing with projections, not proof. In previous seasons, Gates' scheduling philosophy might have afforded more time to tinker and sort out the rotation. This campaign won't afford the same luxury.

Still, scattered throughout those modest minutes are clues about what each player might provide — and, just as importantly, what Gates would need to put around him to make it work.

Bryson Tiller: Versatility — With a Tradeoff

The last time Tiller saw extended time at the five, it overlapped with four minutes as Houston began to pull away in the Big 12 Tournament semifinal.

JoJo Tugler walled off the redshirt freshman from a Mercy Miller drive, then backed him down and spun around a wall-up for an easy bucket. The next trip, Tiller reacted late to Chris Cenac flashing to the mid-post for a soft jumper.

But that sequence didn't raise Kansas coach Bill Self's ire. Barely two minutes in, Tiller let Tugler collect a miss despite having an ideal box-out position. Self immediately called a timeout. At halftime, he pulled Tiller.

"Well, my message is to rebound and play competitive," Self said afterward . "That's it. Be physical, rebound, play competitive. … It's been the message for a long time."

That withering assessment, at least to the west, has shaped the final impression of Tiller's stint in Lawrence.

Reducing Tiller's profile to physicality and rebounding obscures another reality: Self never stopped experimenting with him at center. Tiller appeared there in every game but one, logged at least five minutes in 22 and routinely served as the lone interior player surrounded by four nominal guards or wings.

There's zero point hiding that the results were terrible. Core lineup combinations with Tiller in the post were strafed for a 118.3 raw defensive rating, per EvanMiya.com, a trend mirrored in games where he received his standard allotment at the five.

Yet the tape isn't a gaffe reel. Our charting identified Tiller as the source of just one primary advantage, while 27 of 30 shots were, at minimum, lightly contested. So how did Tiller wind up linked with such putrid outcomes?

Reviewing season-long data also deepens the contradiction. Tiller surrendered 0.813 PPP and ranked in the 74th percentile nationally, per Synergy Sports, while conceding just 0.713 PPP as the terminal defender of ball screens, isolations and post-ups. The tools ($) explain why. Tiller flips his hips, maintains cushion, recovers with length and can survive switches or crossmatches that might sink other bigs.

But look at what happened when he logged his minutes as the sole big. That leaves a frustrating paradox: If Tiller can handle those jobs, why is the accounting so poor?

Exploring Tiller's switching starts to untangle the wires. With him at center, it was treated as an automatic decision to counteract a ball screen. It could snuff out the initial advantage, but at a cost: Tiller left the lane. Tre White slid down from the wing to slot in as a small-ball four, yet rarely replaced him as the low man. Self's group instead relied heavily on weak-side rotations.

Watch the packet twice. The first viewing demonstrates that Tiller is more than functional in space. On the second, watch how KU organizes itself behind him. Frequently, the possession's success has little to do with Tiller.

Charting those possessions made rim replacement the loudest structural signal. When the rim remained protected, Kansas usually survived. When it didn't, every possession in the sample ended in a score. Tiller's versatility only worked if somebody else picked up his shift in the lane.

The second clip provides a textbook illustration. Tiller catch-hedges Cayden Boozer, but White doesn't fully recover and essentially passes off the job to Tiller in a late switch. The sequence saddles Tiller with two poor choices: commit to Boozer and permit an easy drop-off pass or continue to give cushion. Ultimately, Boozer keeps his pace, uses the rim as a shield and converts.

Unfortunately, not every breach can be traced to the scheme. Sometimes Tiller was the last line of defense and, as Self pointed out, didn't act like one.

The miscues vary — a passive wall-up, a missed rotation, positioning a step too high above the restricted area — but the first cut-up shows Tiller can do the job. Consistency is the next step.

That's even more apparent when you study Tiller's handiwork guarding post-ups. Our charted film set captured four examples, and they resulted in just one point. In some ways, Self's frustration is easy to understand. Tiller doesn't sweat absorbing contact, contesting vertically and allowing off-ball help to rotate. And any issues rarely stemmed from an opposing center simply displacing him

For MU, lessening some of the structural strain starts by surrounding Tiller with more positional size. Carey, Burns, Mark Mitchell and Toni Bryant provide it, and even a four-guard alignment could feature a bigger wing like Trent Pierce. That matters on the glass, too. At Kansas, Tiller was often pulled outside optimal rebounding position. For example, our diagnostic sample contained 12 rebound opportunities, and only two were solely Tiller's responsibility. (He secured both.) Yes, he can be more assertive, but lineup construction matters.

The subtler question is how frequently MU switches with Tiller. At pro day, its default ball-screen coverage asked bigs to play at the level or softly hedge, with switches used more selectively. Its off-ball defenders also sit near the midline, positioning them to help aggressively behind the action.

None of that magically turns Tiller into a backline anchor. He still must clean up his low-man lapses, and MU's aggressive help has introduced its own problems. But the structure could ask him to spend less time doing what caused Kansas so much trouble: guarding someone 22 feet from the basket while leaving nobody behind to replace him.

Tiller is probably less a solution to rim protection than a way to change the terms of engagement. His versatility expands Missouri's options; the wager is that its size and help structure can preserve the back line when those tools take him elsewhere.

Yet that's not how coach Rick Barnes used him on Rocky Top.

Instead, the veteran soaked up just 11.9% of Tennessee's available minutes at the five, spending most of last season as the third option behind Felix Okpara and JP Estrella. Barnes only upped that dosage when injuries or foul trouble forced his hand. But while Carey's exposure fluctuated, there's evidence he can be useful when called upon.

Representative lineups accounting for 80% of Carey's minutes conceded 99.7 points per 100 possessions, per EvanMiya.com. That was a slight improvement over the same groups with Okpara in the mix, a hint that Carey can step into an elite defensive shell without compromising it.

Play-type data from games where Carey had his usual shift in the post reinforced that impression. Opponents managed just 0.947 points per possession, but the more revealing detail was how rarely Carey was the culprit for generating a clean advantage.

In that sample, Carey yielded only one advantage, while 16 of 18 shots UT allowed were, at worst, lightly contested. We can't extrapolate those results across an entire season, but it buttresses the notion that Carey wasn't a routine culprit in breakdowns. At a minimum, Carey could diagnose an action, stay connected and give the Vols a chance to see out the trip.

Crucially, Carey wasn't alone on the frontline.

Barnes frequently paired him up with DeWayne Brown II, a 6-foot-7, 247-pound freshman, forging a burly two-big tandem. In those configurations, Carey wasn't moored to the restricted area. In our sample, he spent 15 possessions plying his trade outside the paint, leaving it to Brown or – at least early in the season – Cade Phillips to offer another layer behind him.

Film explains some of that geography. Carey routinely defaulted to drop coverage, and while the results were mixed, the tape gives us a nuanced explanation. Sitting in drop kept the action in front of Carey, giving him a buffer to absorb drives, maintain balance and use his brawny frame to occupy space instead of chasing action. Were there occasions when a roller sealed him off? Yes. But in proper sequence, Carey's ballast didn't drag him down.

That was probably the prudent approach on Barnes' part.

Complications cropped up when more aggressive coverages demanded Carey execute multiple assignments in quick succession. Take the final clip in the packet above. Against Kentucky, Carey hard-hedged a slot pick-and-roll, forcing a long recovery that shifted the burden to Nate Ament, who had to rotate over, wall up and thwart Brandon Garrison.

Carey also had to endure some selective switches. The tape, brief as it is, revealed some encouraging moments: a strong recovery to contest a dribble 3, a competent first slide to force a difficult pull-up late in the shot clock, and a possession where he stayed attached long enough to contest a rim attack from behind.

Those snippets don't erase questions about how Carey would hold up against a steady diet of switches. Or in the more demanding ball-screen coverages that MU prefers. That distinction reappears when assessing Carey's work off the ball.

It's critical to know that Carey was rarely the source of a breakdown. Yet his response to them could be mixed. For example, the film sample below includes a trip where Otega Oweh, a power driver, blew past a smaller defender in Ja'Kobi Gillespie. What did Carey do? He waved his arm in the general direction instead of legitimately stunting into the gap. The next cut-up, from the same game, displays better effort, followed by Carey strongly contesting a spot-up.

Still, a meaningful gap remains between Carey doing one job and carrying an entire possession. Earlier this offseason, we explored how Carey proved vulnerable ($) when he had to execute multiple tasks. Ball screens that made him a helper, tagger or closeout defender made his timing less reliable as responsibilities piled up.

Simply sliding him down the positional ladder to the post isn't a remedy.

Even that role requires guardrails. Obviously, matchups hold some sway. Carey's best suited against opposing big men who, like him, lack overwhelming length or vertical pop. Drop coverage should probably be the default. And the margin for error improves when guards contain dribble penetration.

In late February, the redshirt freshman certainly gave the impression he was ascending toward a breakout . Yet it didn't take long for that appraisal to look as rosy as it was premature.

Sure, Burns still averaged roughly 10 minutes per game over the season's final four contests. But he only posted 1.5 points and 1.8 rebounds, while the opponents outscored MU by 27 points with him on the floor. Then, MU swiftly imported Tiller and Carey to fortify the rotation. Toss in the arrival of five-star freshman Toni Bryant, and Burns finds himself needing to scale the depth chart — again.

His place in the pecking order, however, doesn't render Burns' defensive profile totally irrelevant. If anything, his modest body of work produced one of the more intriguing profiles in the rotation.

The most common lineups with Burns slotted in the post allowed 115.9 points per 100 possessions. To be very clear, that's not a gleaming figure. At the same time, using Shawn Phillips Jr. didn't produce a dramatic swing. The gap – only 2.4 points per 100 possessions – was slender.

Unlike Carey, Burns amassed his body of work as MU's lone five. More interestingly, a review of data from games where he logged his median workload shows opponents averaged only 0.920 points per trip. Through that prism, Burns can look more like a long, sinewy solution.

The crux of his case is the same as it was several months ago: positional defense. In almost half the possessions in the sample, Burns functioned as the low man, and the Tigers conceded only 0.846 PPP. On film, these aren't the most dynamic sequences: Burns lingers around the restricted arc, defends vertically and makes drivers or bigs do real-time geometry proofs to deal with his length.

It's not a montage of swats. Burns merely occupies the right patch of real estate. Often, he was patching a breach instead of causing one. In none of the 21 possessions where we could identify an initial advantage did we pin it on Burns.

Since Burns committed, one of the most persistent questions has been how quickly he can put on good weight and add functional strength. That process was still ongoing, and the consequences also emerged on film. Sometimes, stronger bigs like Florida's Rueben Chinyelu or Arkansas' Malique Ewin used their bodies to seal off Burns from the position he coveted. The leverage they exerted also doubled as a de facto box out.

The rest of his portfolio is mundane. Still, Burns reminded us that discipline is a work in progress, turning sound wall-ups into fouls or goaltends by hunting a block. Meanwhile, his teammates didn't always snatch the misses he created. If Burns hopes to scrap his way toward more minutes, trusting his length and snatching more rebounds might be more material than his value in PNR defense.

None of this makes Burns the favorite to solve MU's center question. That said, he's still useful insurance. Of the vets on the roster, his sample, albeit small, is the cleanest glimpse of a true backline anchor. Should his role remain small, that's handy depth, and there's potentially a foundation to build on.

Diverse as these options are, none of them present Gates a tidy answer.

Again, Tiller, Carey and Burns each spent last season handling only a fraction of a starter's workload. All of them also come with clear questions. Yet the fifth-year coach isn't working with three ill-fitting choices, either. Their utility simply manifests in different ways.

Tiller bestows Gates tactical flexibility, provided MU's defensive shell routinely has someone minding the backline when he ventures to the perimeter. By contrast, Carey's a more conventional option, albeit one who might require MU to be slightly more restrained with the pressure it applies on the ball. With Burns, the job description is niche: stay near the rim, play vertically and wrangle whatever drive breaks contain.

Reasons for cautious optimism also exist. Across all the film troves, first-line breakdowns rarely originated with the big man. It was more common to see one of Tiller, Carey or Burns inherit a problem and repair the damage – a vital distinction considering the Tigers made a habit last season of putting those bigs in binds. Theoretically, Gates' retrofit buttons up the point of attack . Just as importantly, he now has three different ways to calibrate the backline behind it.

Of course, that work means little if MU can't finish the possession.

Rebounding repeatedly surfaced as the final pressure point in our review. The Tigers can execute a coverage, rotate on time and force a difficult attempt. But all that work goes for naught if the opponent collects the miss. For a frontcourt without a proven full-time anchor, those final two seconds might matter every bit as much as the first 20.

Maybe that's the larger wager Gates made this offseason. He didn't necessarily find one veteran capable of blotting out every stain. Instead, he might have assembled enough complementary pieces to prevent the first crack from becoming a full-blown breakdown.

articles.title: Penfield volleyball poised to pursue twin Section V titles
articles.summary: Expectations for the Section V high school volleyball payoffs are high at Penfield, and for good reason.
articles.body:
PENFIELD – Expectations for the Section V high school volleyball playoffs are high at Penfield, and for good reason.

Both the Patriot boys and girls have enjoyed standout seasons in 2026. Both have been mainstays in the state rankings in their respective classifications.

Sectional play will soon begin for both squads. We checked in with each team to ask about postseason preparations and more.

Penfield played in the past two NYSPHSAA Class A boys volleyball finals, winning in 2024 before losing last season.

No opponent has stood in the undefeated Patriots' way this season. They've stayed atop the New York Volleyball Coaches Association's Division 1 state rankings all fall.

Watch above as Owen Gutman and Jake Buckpitt detail the team's success after its Oct. 20 sweep of Fairport, one which required a substantial comeback during the second set. That win moved the Patriots' record to 13-0.

One word sits on the back of each Penfield girls volleyball player's warmup: Kaizen.

Japanese in origin, the term means consistent improvement each day. It's this year's team motto for one of the Section V favorites in Class AAA.

Penfield, which finished the regular season 12-3, seeks its first section title since 2016. Watch below as Natalie Schneider and Lily Spector share details on the team's success after its Oct. 19 win at Rush-Henrietta.

Penfield, Rush-Henrietta battle in Section V girls volleyball

Jeff Uveino joined the USA Today Network in 2023 and began covering Rochester-area high school sports in 2026. He is a graduate of St. Bonaventure University's Jandoli School of Communication and native of Perry. Contact him at juveino@usatodayco.com . articles.title: 3 Nets takeaways from 110-103 loss to Naz Reid, Hornets to open season
articles.summary: Here are three takeaways for the Brooklyn Nets following Wednesday's 110-103 loss to Naz Reid and the Charlotte Hornets to open the 2026-27 season.
articles.body:
NEW YORK -- The Brooklyn Nets (0-1) began their 60th season showing off their classic uniform and going through all of the eras of Nets basketball to get fans excited for the upcoming season. Brooklyn can always put on a good show, especially after a legend like Vince Carter addresses the crowd before a game, but the Charlotte Hornets (1-0) got the better of the Nets .

The Nets lost to the Hornets on Wednesday 110-103 despite the fact that Brooklyn seemed within striking distance for the majority of the game thanks to their two stars. Forward Julius Randle had 33 points, eight rebounds, and seven assists while forward Michael Porter Jr. had 26 points and seven rebounds as the Nets couldn't get much offensive production out of anybody else outside of those two.

In addition to the overall offensive struggles, the Nets also had plenty of defensive issues as they allowed the Hornets to score 20 second-chance points and guard Grayson Allen to pile up 21 points off the bench. Brooklyn had hoped for a win after all of the pageantry heading into the game, but they will have to play better if they're going to win more games than they did last season.

Julius Randle Could Be One Of The Missing Pieces

When Randle was acquired by the Nets via trade from the Minnesota Timberwolves, the question became what kind of player he would be for a young team that was led by Michael Porter Jr. and Egor Demin last season. In the season-opener against the Hornets, Randle showed his ability to affect the game in multiple ways and could be the driving force of a positive season.

Michael Porter Jr. Does It On Both Ends Of The Court

Porter had a slow start to this game as he had just six points in the first half, but he quickly turned that around in the third quarter as he had 12 points in the quarter. In addition to finishing the game with 26 points, Porter also had plenty of impact on the defensive end of the floor as he racked up three steals by using his length to be disruptive in the passing lanes.

The NBA has also been tough for young point guards and this season, it seems that the Nets will be playing three of them: Egor Demin, Mikel Brown Jr., and Nolan Traore. While Brown had the best performance of the trip, he still had some moments where he looked like he was speeding up to get to his spots, but that is understandable. The hope is that Demin will shoot better as the season goes on and that Traore can settle down when the ball is in his hands.

articles.title: Steelers receive great injury news for Week 7 Paris game vs. Saints
articles.summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers received some great Week 7 injury news pertaining to DeShon Elliott's possible return after a 16-game absence.
articles.body:
Fans of the Pittsburgh Steelers , rejoice! The team received a massive injury update ahead of the Week 7 Paris matchup against the New Orleans Saints .

Courtesy of the Steelers ' Week 7 injury report , we learned that safety DeShon Elliott, who missed the final 10 games of the 2025 season and began 2026 on injured reserve, was a full participant in practice on Wednesday. This is incredible news for Elliott's availability and strongly hints at a Week 7 return against the Saints in Paris.

Elliott, who signed with the Steelers in 2024, had an incredible debut season with Pittsburgh and earned himself a two-year extension in June 2025. Unfortunately, his second year with the Steelers didn't go as planned, and he missed 12 total games in 2025, including a season-ending hyperextended knee and hamstring tear.

If his practice participation on Wednesday wasn't enough to leave fans confident about a Week 7 comeback, the Steelers also made a key roster move that all but points to Elliott returning in Paris.

articles.title: ACC injury report for Clemson vs. Virginia Tech: Who is out?
articles.summary: Clemson will be without 10 players against Virginia Tech, including freshman receiver Gordon Sellars, who entered concussion protocol.
articles.body:
Clemson football's initial availability report carries 10 injuries, one being fresh. Freshman wide receiver Gordon Sellars III is the only newly announced absence ahead of Saturday night's game against Virginia Tech, while most of the remaining names have been unavailable for weeks.

Sellars suffered a concussion and entered protocol following what Dabo Swinney described as the freshman's best practice of the season. Clemson will hold him out when the Tigers host the Hokies at 7 p.m. ET on ESPN.

The 6-foot-3, 200-pound receiver had finally worked his way back from the hamstring issue that limited him during fall camp. Swinney said Sellars made two impressive catches during practice and had established himself as Clemson's fourth receiver behind Bryant Wesco Jr., Tyler Brown and T.J. Moore.

Sellars has only three catches for eight yards this season, so Clemson is not losing a premium part of its passing game. His absence still shortens a receiver rotation that is already missing Cole Turner and reserve Chase Byrd. Turner has been away from the program since fall camp while handling a personal matter

There is some good health news from the report. Running back Jay Haynes returned against Charleston Southern for his first game action since suffering multiple knee injuries in the 2024 ACC Championship Game. Defensive tackle Kourtney Kelly also made his Clemson debut after tearing his ACL during spring practice.

Virginia Tech has its own problems up front. Offensive lineman Justin Terry is out, while Nathaniel Wright, Lucas Austin, and Montavious Cunningham are questionable. The Hokies allowed seven sacks in last week's 34-24 victory over Georgia Tech .
